parts.note: to engage a ship or coach is to charter it
a house is a building

explanation.surface: Someone hires premises to open a school.
explanation.walkthrough: CHARTERHOUSE is a famous English public school, founded in London in 1611 and later moved to Surrey.
explanation.definitionFit: Charterhouse is the name of a well-known English public school.

explanation.surface: A Norman champion among conkers.
explanation.definitionFit: William of Normandy is known as the Conqueror; in the British children's game of conkers, a horse chestnut that has beaten many others is called a conqueror.

parts.note: asks for the first name of Leigh, the hero of Charles Kingsley's novel Westward Ho!

explanation.definitionFit: The hero of Kingsley's Westward Ho! is Amyas Leigh, so his forename is what the clue wants.

clue.text: One must draw the line at-this

definitions.text: One must draw the line at-this

parts.words: One must draw the line at-this
parts.note: the idiom 'draw the line at' means refuse, but here the activity is literally drawing over lines on a transparent sheet

explanation.surface: A statement of a limit one will not go beyond.
explanation.definitionFit: Copying a picture through thin paper means drawing along every line of the original.

annotationWithheld.why: Behind the time in colour: LATE in RED gives the letters, but no clue word defines RELATED

clue.text: Bury is the place for these

definitions.text: Bury is the place for these

parts.words: Bury is the place for these
parts.note: Bury reads as the Lancashire town, but in lower case burying is where funeral rites end

explanation.surface: A remark that some events belong in the Lancashire town of Bury.
explanation.walkthrough: Bury is a town near Manchester; the capital letter hides the verb 'bury'.
explanation.definitionFit: Funeral rites are held when the dead are put in the ground.

parts.note: canonization makes someone a saint, abbreviated ST
singular means one in number

explanation.surface: A single act of sainthood that is very influential.
explanation.walkthrough: The stone is a British unit of weight, fourteen pounds.
explanation.definitionFit: A stone is a unit of weight used in Britain, and a heavy rock also weighs a lot.

parts.note: bitter is a kind of English beer, so its very last drop is the close of the pint

explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means the very finish of something hard; bitter is also a British ale.

clue.text: Condition of Andy when brought to book

definitions.text: Condition of Andy when brought to book

parts.words: Condition of Andy when brought to book
parts.note: Samuel Lover's novel is titled ... Andy, so in the book Andy carries this adjective

explanation.surface: Someone called Andy is in trouble when he is held to account.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brought to book' suggests being punished; here it means put into a book, Samuel Lover's 1842 novel Handy Andy.
explanation.definitionFit: In the novel title the hero is described as convenient and useful, which is his state.

parts.note: a plain definition: indirect mentions of something

explanation.definitionFit: Passing mentions of something are indirect references to it.

clue.text: Enough on the workshop in Anglo-Latin

definitions.text: Enough on the workshop in Anglo-Latin

indicators.note: on means the first piece is placed on top of, ahead of, the next one

parts.note: satis is the Latin word for enough, the Latin half of the hybrid
a factory is an industrial workshop, the English half

explanation.surface: A Latin scholar's note about a factory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in Anglo-Latin' tells you the word joins Latin SATIS to English FACTORY, and as a whole it means 'enough', as satis itself does.
explanation.definitionFit: Something adequate is enough for the purpose.

clue.text: Not for sports wear at Oxford, nor yet Dublin (two words)

definitions.text: Not for sports wear at Oxford, nor yet Dublin

parts.words: Not for sports wear at Oxford, nor yet Dublin
parts.note: an Oxford sportsman wins a Blue, and in 1930s Dublin the ... were a political movement wearing that colour

explanation.surface: Advice on clothing that does not suit either Oxford sport or Dublin.
explanation.walkthrough: The Blueshirts were the Irish fascist-style movement of the 1930s, and a Blue is the award for representing Oxford or Cambridge at sport.
explanation.definitionFit: A garment of that colour suggests both the Oxford sporting award and the Irish political movement.

parts.note: put CON in front of this word and it names what William of Normandy did in 1066

explanation.surface: Someone was swindled by a Norman.
explanation.walkthrough: With CON before it this word becomes the Norman Conquest, the deed of the 1-down hero; 'Conned' looks like 'cheated'.
explanation.definitionFit: A search becomes a conquest once the prefix is added.

parts.note: a 'record performance' sounds like a best-ever feat, but it is what a gramophone disc does on the turntable

explanation.surface: A best-ever achievement.
explanation.definitionFit: A gramophone disc revolves on the turntable while it plays.

parts.note: Frank looks like a man's name, but frank as an adjective has another word meaning the same

explanation.surface: A man called Frank goes by another name.
explanation.definitionFit: Being frank means being open and candid, and another name for that quality is the answer.

explanation.surface: Societies set up for people in transport.
explanation.definitionFit: A golfer's longest wood is a club for tee shots, and people at the wheel of buses or lorries also work in transport.

parts.note: the idiom means someone who fulfils promises, but read literally it is a lad carrying shopping

explanation.surface: Praise for someone reliable.
explanation.definitionFit: A shop lad who carries orders to customers literally delivers goods.

indicators.note: a grenade that bursts flies to pieces, so its letters are scattered and rearranged

explanation.surface: A grenade exploding, as if in a fury.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone furious is filled with anger.

parts.note: a plain definition: drawings or schemes

explanation.definitionFit: Plans and drawings are both blueprints or schemes.

indicators.note: missing means the following letters are absent from the country name

parts.note: the Commonwealth of Australia is that country's official name

indicators.note: nearly means the word all loses its last letter

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Almost the whole Commonwealth has gone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nearly' cuts ALL to AL, and 'missing' takes AL out of AUSTRALIA.
explanation.definitionFit: The Alpine republic is itself a commonwealth, a self-governing state.

parts.note: bridge is a card game

explanation.surface: A game reduced to its essence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Epitome' is used here as a verb, an old form of 'epitomise', to cut down to a summary.
explanation.definitionFit: To epitomise a text is to shorten and condense it.

clue.text: Marbles evidently don't agree with Nigel

indicators.note: letters that do not agree with the order in the name are out of line, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A boy called Nigel quarrels over his game of marbles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'don't agree with' rearranges NIGEL. The Elgin Marbles are the Parthenon sculptures in the British Museum, named after Lord Elgin.
explanation.definitionFit: The Parthenon sculptures in London are named the Elgin Marbles, so the name stands for them.

annotationWithheld.why: Phonetically window relish: 'window' heard as WIND-O with wind giving GUST is a synonym inside a sounded word, which the grammar cannot express

clue.text: With him all is colloquially well (two words)

definitions.text: With him all is colloquially well

parts.words: With him all is colloquially well
parts.note: refers to the Victorian catchphrase 'all ...', meaning everything is in order

explanation.surface: A man whose presence makes everything right.
explanation.walkthrough: The general Sir Garnet Wolseley was so efficient that 'all Sir Garnet' became British slang for 'all correct'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Victorian phrase named after General Wolseley means everything is fine.

parts.note: scot is an old word for a tax, as in scot-free

explanation.surface: Naturally, a levy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of course' reads as 'naturally', but means 'belonging to a course': Ascot is the racecourse in Berkshire.
explanation.definitionFit: Ascot is a famous English racecourse, so it is a thing of the turf.

parts.note: after three days inside the whale, the biblical Jonah was spat out onto land

explanation.definitionFit: The great fish vomited Jonah up, ejecting him from its belly.

clue.text: Is it appropriately made from pitchpine?

definitions.text: Is it appropriately made from pitchpine?

parts.words: Is it appropriately made from pitchpine?
parts.note: pitch pine is a timber, but split it as 'pitch' (throw) and 'pine' and it fits the Highland pole that is thrown

explanation.surface: A question about the timber used for something.
explanation.walkthrough: At Highland games in Scotland a long pole, usually of pine, is tossed end over end.
explanation.definitionFit: The pole thrown at Highland games is a pitched length of pine.

indicators.note: the printed abbreviation for anagram says the two words before it are rearranged

explanation.surface: A remark that tennis is an expensive game.
explanation.walkthrough: An old-style clue with no definition: '(anag.)' rearranges COSTLY TENNIS.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something consistently means doing it steadily and regularly.
